Nicolette stood by the sutler’s wagon, the chrome glint of her new satchel glaring under the fading sun. She needed it to look as if it had survived the Civil War, preferably without smelling like a factory. Peregrine stirred his dye pot, the steam carrying the scent of wet walnut and old wood.

“How do I knock fifty years off this satchel by tomorrow?”

He didn’t look up, just lifted the wooden spoon. “Fifty years forward, you mean. First rule: nothing on it fresher than saddle soap and sunlight.”

Nicolette checked her watch, then his apron, stained with decades of iron mordant. “You’ve got six sentences before my attention span files for disability.”

Peregrine set the spoon down, splashing dark liquid. “Walnut-husk bath, flex dry, drag it behind a bike for fifty yards, rub with fireplace ash, finish with lanolin while warm.”

She wrinkled her nose at the suggestion of ash. “Fireplace ash sounds like stage dressing, not functional aging.”

“Ash is very fine grit; it shears the grain fuzz so the dye bites evenly.” He tapped the rim of his tin cup.

“Do I soak the whole thing or just daub?”

“Submerge two minutes, squeeze, let it dry crumpled; bending while damp makes stress creases look earned.”

Nicolette imagined the stench of wet decay clinging to her backpack. “Won’t the walnut stink of rot?”

“Smells like tannin and riverbanks; add a splash of pennyroyal if you mind tourists sniffing.”

She glanced toward the main thoroughfare, where a straggler lingered near the fry-bread stand. “My committee head hates anachronisms. Any shortcuts that don’t involve dragging leather?”

“Ball it up in a towel and knead; beats bicycle chain oil stains from last year.”

Nicolette nodded, visualizing the friction. “Documentation demands provenance detail—what if someone asks?”

Peregrine leaned back, resting his hands on his knees. “Say it belonged to a post courier, spent weeks under wagon tarps, scraped by harness hardware—those scratches prove themselves.”

She pulled a blank leather tag from her pocket. “I need written steps; scrawl them on this tag and I’m gone.”

He took the tag, dipping his finger in the dye to write. “Done—remember picture first, then patina; historians trust the story, not the sheen.”

Nicolette tucked the wet tag into her pocket, satisfied. “Perfect. If my adviser gripes, I’m blaming the walnut guy.”

Peregrine smiled, picking up his cup. “I’ll be at the forge; bring coffee and I’ll sign an affidavit of authenticity.”

She turned toward the path, the satchel suddenly feeling less like a prop and more like an artifact waiting to happen.

plan:
Late October, 3:45 p.m. The community-arts office is a reclaimed garage whose big rollup door is jammed half-open; autumn air drifts in laced with turpentine and leaf-smoke. Outside, the freshly painted poem wall—twenty metres of brick scarred with stencilled couplets—faces west, already chalking in the low sun. Inside, paint samples bloom like defunct postage stamps across a scuffed trestle table. A battered shop heater clicks off, leaving the concrete floor cold enough to numb boot soles.

Nikolai, coat still on, has a meeting with his advisor at four. His canvas satchel sags with library books about “public text durability.” He wants the shortest route from Question to Answer so he can catch the cross-campus bus.

Odettea, wearing a denim apron tattooed with technicolour smudges, has spent the morning patching last summer’s mural bleaches. She warms her knuckles around a chipped enamel mug of chicory coffee and enjoys the company; most people assume varnish is boring until their artwork flakes off in hand-sized sheets.

Physical anchors they’ll orbit: a quart can of matte UV-blocking varnish (label sun-bleached to ambiguity) and the office’s salvaged bay window, through which both watch a loose sheet of printer paper scuff across the brick wall, illustrating how quickly weather strips pigment.

The encounter’s shape: inquiry → clarification → options → conclusion. No revelations, just a graduate student trying not to freeze his grant-funded poem wall into ruin and a craftsperson offering grounded advice while the afternoon light drains away.
dialogue:
Nikolai: I’ve got painted text going up on that south-facing brick—do I seal it now or regret it all winter?
Odettea: You seal it now. Freeze-thaw pops paint off like soda tabs.
Nikolai: That fast? Temperatures haven’t hit zero yet.
Odettea: Brick stores water. One cold night and it expands, poem becomes potato chips.
Nikolai: So what do I roll on? The budget’s gone except for thirty bucks and grad-student coupons.
Odettea: Polishethane 500. One coat, matte finish, UV blockers already inside. Thirty covers your square footage.
Nikolai: Someone told me marine spar varnish breathes better.
Odettea: Spar’s great for boats; on brick it stays stretchy and grabs grime. You’ll scrub the words off cleaning it.
Nikolai: I heard breathing matters.
Odettea: Wall respiration is folklore. You want vapor out, not hydrocarbons in. Modern polyurethanes micro-vent; they’re fine.
Nikolai: Satin or gloss?
Odettea: Matte. Sun glare off satin turns letters into chrome mirrors by November.
Nikolai: And temperature window?
Odettea: Air needs to stay above ten Celsius for four hours. You’ve got today and maybe tomorrow before the front.
Nikolai: I can start at dawn.
Odettea: Better start now; daylight’s shrinking faster than grant money. Stir, don’t shake—bubbles dry white.
Nikolai: One coat really enough?
Odettea: Two’s safer, but if supplies are tight one heavy coat plus touch-up in spring beats nothing.
Nikolai: Edge first or field?
Odettea: Cut in edges with a brush, roll the middle, keep a wet line or you’ll lap marks spelling mistakes.
Nikolai: Humidity tonight’s forecast at eighty percent—problem?
Odettea: Eighty slows cure, won’t stop it. Just don’t tarp it; trapped moisture turns the varnish milky like bad tea.
Nikolai: Brushes clean with mineral spirits?
Odettea: Yep. Two-step: rinse in spirits, then dish soap, or tomorrow they’re plastic fossils.
Nikolai: Thanks. If my advisor asks, I’ll blame you for the fumes.
Odettea: Tell her it’s archival; committees love the A-word.

plan: The office sits behind a double-sealed door off Corridor C-3 in the low-rise block of Pacific Proteins. Fluorescent tubes hum overhead, and the air tastes faintly of soy steam that leaked from the pilot plant. It’s 8:15 a.m.; first production run starts at nine. A whiteboard leans against one cinder-block wall, half-erased scribbles showing pH targets from last week’s kimchi sausage experiment. Declan, resident food-safety tech and unofficial HACCP whisperer, is already at the desk, coffee mug bearing the logo “REMEMBER TO CALIBRATE.” He enjoys untangling forms; it feels like solving a crossword where the answer keeps people out of hospital. Farah, M.Sc. candidate, rushes in with a clipboard she printed at 3 a.m.; her thesis adviser told her “get Declan’s signature or find another plant.” She’s spent the night color-coding hazard tables, but the tofu brine step still feels like blank space on the page. Her goal: walk out with approvals, no footnotes. Motivation is simple—graduate, stay sane. She’s ready to argue if Declan drifts into anecdotes. Declan notices the frayed stress-ball hanging from her lanyard; he suspects she’s one nudge from spinning it like a centrifuge. Two objects matter: the clipboard stack and Declan’s battered copy of the CFIA HACCP guide that he props open like a preacher’s bible. Outside the single window, steam plumes rise from the tofu curdling tanks, drifting past like tired ghosts clocking off shift. The encounter shape is linear: Farah hands over the checklist, Declan reads through each critical control point aloud, she challenges anything that smells like delay, and he answers with measured corrections. No surprise inspections or alarms—just two people negotiating line items while the clock ticks toward production.
dialogue:
Farah: Morning—can you bless these CCPs before the nine-o’clock batch? The tofu brine tank looks iffy to me.
Declan: Let’s walk through it. First page says you’re flagging brine temperature; good instinct. What’s your target and critical limit?
Farah: Above 72 °C to knock out coliforms, but we’re reading 68 °C on probe 3. How hot do you actually need?
Declan: 72 minimum, but you also need a one-minute come-up time logged. Bump your set-point to 75; the tank overshoots two degrees when it’s this cold outside.
Farah: Overshoot allowance isn’t on the form. Will an auditor buy a handwritten note?
Declan: Attach the calibration record for that probe—today’s date on the sticker. Auditors hate mystery; they love paperwork trails.
Farah: Already stickered, but space is tight. Can I reference the logbook number instead of reprinting data?
Declan: Reference is fine, just write “Logbook QA-4, page today’s date, line 12-18.” No room for interpretation.
Farah: Done. Next, metal detection—last shift found nothing, but the new tofu formulation’s denser. Sensitivity still 2 mm ferrous?
Declan: Bump to 1.5 mm. Dense curd can hide thin wires. Test every hour, not just start-up, and record three passes—fail the middle one on purpose to prove rejection works.
Farah: Intentional fail every hour? Maintenance will grumble.
Declan: Let them grumble; it beats a recall. Note the test-piece batch number on the sheet—auditors always ask which piece you used.
Farah: Okay. Last snag: chilled brine hold. I’ve got five-hour limit in the hazard chart; QA manager says six is fine.
Declan: Five keeps you safe if the glycol chiller burps. Six is betting weather. Stick to five and you’ll never explain bacterial growth to a review board.
Farah: Plant manager wants throughput. Five means smaller batches.
Declan: Smaller batches beat production freeze when CFIA slaps a hold. Your signature, your neck—keep it at five.
Farah: Fair enough. Anything else before I sign off?
Declan: Date every correction in red; initials beside each. If it’s not in red, an auditor pretends it never happened.
Farah: Red pen, got it. Appreciate the quick audit; I’ll have revised sheets to you in twenty.
Declan: Bring coffee; page seven always dehydrates me. We’ll stamp them and you’re golden.

Farah’s pen scratched loudly as she made the note, the sound aggressive in the quiet office. “Okay. Last snag: chilled brine hold. I’ve got five-hour limit in the hazard chart; QA manager says six is fine.”

Declan looked toward the window, where gray plumes of steam rose from the vats beyond the glass, drifting like tired ghosts. “Five keeps you safe if the glycol chiller burps. Six is betting weather. Stick to five and you’ll never explain bacterial growth to a review board.”

Farah’s jaw tightened, the stress-ball on her lanyard swinging in a small, agitated arc. “Plant manager wants throughput. Five means smaller batches.”

“Smaller batches beat production freeze when CFIA slaps a hold. Your signature, your neck—keep it at five.”

She exhaled, long and slow, the tension draining from her shoulders just a fraction. “Fair enough. Anything else before I sign off?”

Declan tapped the margin of the page with his index finger. “Date every correction in red; initials beside each. If it’s not in red, an auditor pretends it never happened.”

Farah swapped her black pen for a bright red one, the cap popping with a satisfying click. “Red pen, got it. Appreciate the quick audit; I’ll have revised sheets to you in twenty.”

Declan picked up his mug, the coffee lukewarm now, and gave a small, weary smile. “Bring coffee; page seven always dehydrates me. We’ll stamp them and you’re golden.”

Kiln day, late afternoon. Unloading happens in the ware room behind the studio, a concrete-floored space that smells of warm bisque and brick dust. Two rolling metal racks stand empty. The test tiles line the far counter, still radiating heat like a tray of fresh cookies.

Iskra stands at the counter edge, gloved fingers drumming against the shelf. Her last batch of underglaze pencil marks came out blank. Two weeks of line-work gone ghost-white in the firing. She has a meeting with her advisor tomorrow and needs a fix tonight.

Jae comes in carrying the kiln log clipboard, sleeves rolled to the elbow. He’s been the kiln tech here three semesters, longer than anyone in the grad cohort. His job right now is logging shelf temps and answering questions for whoever’s hovering, which today means Iskra.

On the counter sits a cracked tile she’s saved: cobalt lines vanished, surface glossy and line-free as a fresh sheet of porcelain. One more tile rests beside it, un-fired, blank side up. There is a test brush and a raku pencil in a water glass, tools that can be claimed or ignored.
dialogue:
Iskra: My pencil lines disappeared in the last firing.
Jae: Underglaze pencil or regular graphite?
Iskra: Underglaze. Cobalt-based, cone 6.
Jae: Those need oxygen to survive the fire.
Iskra: I left them uncovered because I didn't want smudging.
Jae: That’s the problem. The pencil layer burns away without flux.
Iskra: So I need to cover them with a clear glaze?
Jae: A thin wash of clear or a soft frit glaze works.
Iskra: Won’t that blur the lines?
Jae: Only if the glaze is too thick. Just kiss the surface.
Iskra: I tried wax resist once. Lines still vanished.
Jae: Wax burns off too early. You need glass.
Iskra: How thin are we talking?
Jae: Thin enough to read newsprint through it if you held it up.
Iskra: Fire once or twice?
Jae: Once. The glaze seals the lines; second fire erases them.
Iskra: What about the hold time?
Jae: Normal bisque cycle. Ten-minute hold at peak is plenty.
Iskra: Works on porcelain too?
Jae: Works better. Porcelain doesn’t breathe.
Iskra: I’ve got a test batch cooling right now.
Jae: Crack the door at two hundred degrees. Don’t shock them.

She had a meeting with her advisor tomorrow, and two weeks of line-work had gone ghost-white in the firing.

Jae entered, carrying the kiln log clipboard. He rolled his sleeves to the elbow, his demeanor calm amidst the cooling racks. He looked at the blank tile, then at Iskra’s tense shoulders.

Jae nodded, tapping the clipboard with a pen. “Underglaze pencil or regular graphite?”

“Underglaze. Cobalt-based, cone 6.”

“Those need oxygen to survive the fire.”

Iskra looked down at her hands. “I left them uncovered because I didn't want smudging.”

“That’s the problem. The pencil layer burns away without flux.”

She picked up the test brush, weighing its balance. “So I need to cover them with a clear glaze?”

“A thin wash of clear or a soft frit glaze works.”

“Won’t that blur the lines?”

“Only if the glaze is too thick. Just kiss the surface.”

Iskra shook her head, frustration tightening her jaw. “I tried wax resist once. Lines still vanished.”

Jae stepped closer, pointing to the glazed tile. “Wax burns off too early. You need glass.”

“How thin are we talking?”

“Thin enough to read newsprint through it if you held it up.”

“Fire once or twice?”

“Once. The glaze seals the lines; second fire erases them.”

Iskra exhaled, the tension leaving her shoulders in a slow wave. “What about the hold time?”

“Normal bisque cycle. Ten-minute hold at peak is plenty.”

“Works on porcelain too?”

“Works better. Porcelain doesn’t breathe.”

She looked at the test batch still glowing faintly in the kiln corner. “I’ve got a test batch cooling right now.”

Jae checked the thermometer dial. “Crack the door at two hundred degrees. Don’t shock them.”

Iskra nodded, dipping the brush into the water glass, ready to try again. The dust motes danced in the late light, settling slowly on the empty metal racks.

The deck stands eight feet above the scruffy backyard, pine boards gray from sun and last winter’s salt. The grill, a three-burner monster from Craigslist, squats beside the rail like a rusting war monument. Soot streaks the lid; inside, black grease has been adding layers since move-in day last September. Late Saturday afternoon, neighborhood lawnmowers have quit and a warm cedar-plank smell drifts over the fence—someone else already eating.

Cormac needs to cook burgers for new downstairs neighbors at six-thirty sharp. His stomach’s tight with a low-grade dread that grease he can’t see will poison somebody. Twenty minutes ago he texted Nalani, grad-school acquaintance from the Materials Slack channel who once mentioned she’d restored a 1974 Weber to working order.

Cormac’s state: Used to following lab protocols, hates open-ended instructions, currently convinced the whole thing will go sideways if he guesses wrong. Wants a clear checklist he can run and then stop worrying.

Nalani’s state: Just finished sanding a jewelry box for a cousin’s graduation, hands smelling faintly of teak oil and orange degreaser. She hopes this grilling favor will lead to borrowing Cormac’s bike rack tomorrow. Cheerful and precise; defaults to chunking advice into numbered steps whenever possible.

Environmental details they can lean on: rusty grill brush hanging from a nail, cracked orange bucket catch-all with half a stainless steel scrub pad inside, next to a gallon jug of Simple Green and a half-empty box of latex gloves. One unmatched garden gnome wearing a cracked fishing hat stares glumly at the mess from the corner of the deck.
dialogue:
Cormac: Hey. The neighbors are coming at six-thirty and this grill hasn’t been cleaned since cavemen invented fire. I need a quick deep-clean, no fluff. Break it down.
Nalani: Kill the gas first—main valve on the tank. Burners off. Wait five minutes for anything to bleed out.
Cormac: Done. What scrapes off the crap?
Nalani: Remove the grates, soak them in a garbage bag with half a cup of ammonia and two cups hot water. Tight twist-tie, let sit fifteen while you hit the inside.
Cormac: Ammonia’s under the sink; got it. Inside’s the sticky part.
Nalani: Ash-vac the loose chunks or just bang them into the orange bucket. Then vacuum again so you’re not scrubbing gravel.
Cormac: Can I use steel wool on the enamel or will that scratch through?
Nalani: Use the stainless pad in the bucket—it’s gentler. Wet it, add a squirt of dish soap, circular motion like you’re waxing a car.
Cormac: Circle, not zigzag. Good. I saw someone else talking about putting the grates on self-clean in the oven. Faster?
Nalani: Only if you want white smoke alarms. Fifteen-minute ammonia bag beats a two-hour vent cycle every time.
Cormac: Bag then rinse. Rinse then do what?
Nalani: Quick towel dry, then run the burners on high ten minutes to burn off any soap film. Lightly oil the grates right after—canola on a paper towel and tongs.
Cormac: That covered it. You’re sure no one’s tasting last semester’s brat fat?
Nalani: Promise. Wipe the lid seal with a damp rag, slap everything back together, fire it up and toss on a sacrificial onion. You’ll smell the difference.

Cormac stood on the gray pine deck, stomach tightening as he stared at the rusting three-burner monstrosity. The grill looked less like an appliance and more like a crime scene preserved in time. A lone garden gnome in a cracked fishing hat watched him from the corner, expressionless. He needed this done fast, and he needed it done right.

“Hey. The neighbors are coming at six-thirty and this grill hasn’t been cleaned since cavemen invented fire. I need a quick deep-clean, no fluff. Break it down.”

Nalani leaned against the railing, hands smelling faintly of teak oil and orange degreaser from her afternoon project. She didn’t smile; she just pointed a finger at the propane tank.

“Kill the gas first—main valve on the tank. Burners off. Wait five minutes for anything to bleed out.”

He turned the valve with a sharp click, then stepped back, checking his watch. “Done. What scrapes off the crap?”

Nalani gestured to the cracked orange bucket sitting near the rail, a stainless steel scrub pad visible inside. “Remove the grates, soak them in a garbage bag with half a cup of ammonia and two cups hot water. Tight twist-tie, let sit fifteen while you hit the inside.”

Cormac nodded, already moving toward the sink. “Ammonia’s under the sink; got it. Inside’s the sticky part.”

“Ash-vac the loose chunks or just bang them into the orange bucket. Then vacuum again so you’re not scrubbing gravel.”

He looked at the rusted brush hanging from the nail, then at the pad. “Can I use steel wool on the enamel or will that scratch through?”

“Use the stainless pad in the bucket—it’s gentler. Wet it, add a squirt of dish soap, circular motion like you’re waxing a car.”

“Circle, not zigzag. Good.” He paused, remembering a forum post he’d read. “I saw someone else talking about putting the grates on self-clean in the oven. Faster?”

Nalani raised an eyebrow, her tone flat. “Only if you want white smoke alarms. Fifteen-minute ammonia bag beats a two-hour vent cycle every time.”

Cormac exhaled, relief washing over him. “Bag then rinse. Rinse then do what?”

“Quick towel dry, then run the burners on high ten minutes to burn off any soap film. Lightly oil the grates right after—canola on a paper towel and tongs.”

He wiped a bead of sweat from his forehead. “That covered it. You’re sure no one’s tasting last semester’s brat fat?”

“Promise.” She tapped the lid. “Wipe the lid seal with a damp rag, slap everything back together, fire it up and toss on a sacrificial onion. You’ll smell the difference.”

The cedar scent from the neighbor’s yard drifted over the fence again, no longer mocking but promising. Cormac picked up the stainless pad.

Late afternoon in the stormwater parking bay on campus, hot white sun bouncing off fresh tarmac. A grid of cylindrical catch-basins lines the rear half of the lot, each bristling with survey stakes like misplaced knitting needles. Rolled plans, a half-empty tray of numbered aggregate samples, and Mirek’s field notebook lay across the open tailgate of a battered red Tacoma. 

Mirek stands still for the first time all day: boots on the pavement, shirt already salt-ringed. He’s been dragging chain and buckets since breakfast, needs to pick the right stone to pass infiltration rates tomorrow’s demo, and keeps getting decimals wrong. His calculator has a cracked screen and his patience has a shorter crack in the same place.

Safa rolls up pushing a hand truck stacked with sealed buckets. She clocked out at noon from the geology lab but came anyway; her dog, an overweight beagle panting under the truck, acts as mascot. She’s cheerful because she likes solving the dumb problems students always present and, secretly, because the storm lab supplies excellent free coffee. She’s ready to use the phrase “capillary break” without sounding like a textbook.

Two props anchor the talk: the tray of sample tubes—clear plastic cylinders with glued-in layers labelled “1A coarse” through “6F fines”—and the cracked digital display on Mirek’s half-bald meter wand that blinks “0.87” and won’t average properly. Between them sits a can of cold brew Safa grabbed on the way over; Mirek will eye it like it’s the last canteen in a desert. Conversation starts polite, skids toward clipped irritation and back to shared purpose as the right aggregate is identified.
dialogue:
Mirek: The runoff from yesterday’s test hit seven mils a minute—way over spec. I swapped fines for coarse at layer three, now the meter coughs up 0.87 cm/hr. That's still too slow.
Safa: Seven mils is slug flow territory. What’s your target?
Mirek: Minimum five cm/hr for Monday’s mock inspection. I’m seeing fines migrating downstream; maybe 1A’s the culprit.
Safa: One-A is gap-graded—looks coarse but nests tight. Run a sieve check; I bet the bedding layer’s choking.
Mirek: Did that, nine ABVs away from perfect, and still it clogs when I backfill. Plotting against ASTM gives me hoops to jump through.
Safa: Switch to a uniformly graded aggregate—say 3D. Angular, open voids, no nesting. Won’t migrate if your geotextile trench is clean.
Mirek: The gradation chart says 3D voids too fast; head’s worried about frost heave minus the STP planting soil layer.
Safa: Place a 25-mm choker layer above 3D. Compacts at ninety-five Proctor, holds frost loads, buys time until bioretention matures.
Mirek: Site specs say 15 mm max for parking bay sections. Twenty-five won’t clear review.
Safa: Then split the lifts—15 mm choker above 3D intermediate, add a 5-mm perforated pipe as underdrain. Inspector loves redundancy.
Mirek: More pipe equals more excavation. We’re already two days behind schedule.
Safa: Less digging than a respawn. Rip the top three inches, top-dress with choker, tamp, and you’re green. Took us thirty minutes on the mall lot last fall.
Mirek: Fine. Do I bake fines into the voids to tighten it up or leave raw aggregates bare?
Safa: Leave raw. Any bunker sand will plug the sieve within three wet events; you’ll be back next month measuring slugs again.
Mirek: Meter still blurs the decimal. Do you trust your wand?
Safa: Mine’s old but reads steady within two percent. Trade field protocols later; I’ll calibrate, you rerun the plot.
Mirek: I’ll owe you twice.
Safa: Pay in cold brew. Dog here drinks the rest, but he’s a cheap date.

Mirek stood rigid on the blistering tarmac, his boots rooted to the fresh black pavement. The afternoon sun reflected off the empty lot with a harsh, white glare, making the grid of cylindrical catch-basins look like a field of misplaced knitting needles. His field notebook lay open on the tailgate of the battered red Tacoma, pages warped by humidity and sweat. He wiped a salt ring from his collar, eyes fixed on the cracked screen of the meter wand blinking a stubborn “0.87.”

“The runoff from yesterday’s test hit seven mils a minute—way over spec. I swapped fines for coarse at layer three, now the meter coughs up 0.87 cm/hr. That's still too slow.”

Safa rolled up, her hand truck groaning under the weight of sealed aggregate buckets. Her beagle, heavy with fur and appetite, panted loudly from beneath the wheelbase. She leaned against the truck, eyeing the half-empty tray of labeled sample tubes with the calm of someone who had solved this problem before.

“Seven mils is slug flow territory. What’s your target?”

“Minimum five cm/hr for Monday’s mock inspection. I’m seeing fines migrating downstream; maybe 1A’s the culprit.”

She picked up a tube labeled 1A, shook it lightly, and set it back down. “One-A is gap-graded—looks coarse but nests tight. Run a sieve check; I bet the bedding layer’s choking.”

Mirek rubbed his temples, the heat pressing behind his eyes. “Did that, nine ABVs away from perfect, and still it clogs when I backfill. Plotting against ASTM gives me hoops to jump through.”

“Switch to a uniformly graded aggregate—say 3D. Angular, open voids, no nesting. Won’t migrate if your geotextile trench is clean.”

He frowned, glancing at the gradation chart taped to the truck’s door. “The gradation chart says 3D voids too fast; head’s worried about frost heave minus the STP planting soil layer.”

Safa pulled a can of cold brew from her bag and slid it across the tailgate. “Place a 25-mm choker layer above 3D. Compacts at ninety-five Proctor, holds frost loads, buys time until bioretention matures.”

Mirek stared at the condensation beading on the aluminum. “Site specs say 15 mm max for parking bay sections. Twenty-five won’t clear review.”

“Then split the lifts—15 mm choker above 3D intermediate, add a 5-mm perforated pipe as underdrain. Inspector loves redundancy.”

“More pipe equals more excavation. We’re already two days behind schedule.”

She shrugged, popping the tab on the second can for herself. “Less digging than a respawn. Rip the top three inches, top-dress with choker, tamp, and you’re green. Took us thirty minutes on the mall lot last fall.”

Mirek took the cold brew, the chill seeping into his palms. “Fine. Do I bake fines into the voids to tighten it up or leave raw aggregates bare?”

“Leave raw. Any bunker sand will plug the sieve within three wet events; you’ll be back next month measuring slugs again.”

He looked at his flickering meter, then at hers, which glowed steady and reliable. “Meter still blurs the decimal. Do you trust your wand?”

“Mine’s old but reads steady within two percent. Trade field protocols later; I’ll calibrate, you rerun the plot.”

Mirek nodded, the tension in his shoulders easing just enough to let him breathe. “I’ll owe you twice.”

“Pay in cold brew. Dog here drinks the rest, but he’s a cheap date.”

The accessioning counter sits under fluorescent tubes that have been humming since six a.m. The air smells faintly of ethanol from the wipes used to swab the benchtops. A stainless-steel tray of blood-collection tubes waits to be tagged; the printer is wedged between two racks on the near wall, its green power light blinking like a metronome stuck on seven-eights time.

Nkechi steps up at seven-twenty with her first rack of the day. She has already spotted the rhythm: every seventh label prints half a line, curls, jams, and costs her a tube she has to fish out and re-label by hand. She is polite, but her patience evaporates like alcohol on plastic. She wants the answer in two sentences, preferably with a button to press.

Florian is on rotation as the “lab tech,” which only means he is the warm body nearest the door when she starts shouting. Off-shift started five minutes ago, and he is still here because his bike lock is frozen solid outside in the Boston winter and he is waiting for the sun to rise another ten degrees. His body leans sideways, one shoulder already pointed toward the exit. He will answer in the shortest legal words that still pass for complete sentences, steering her toward someone who is not him.

On the counter between them lie two objects that will keep coming up: the roll of shiny white labels, edge slightly scuffed where the seventh one keeps ripping, and the laminated troubleshooting card taped to the wall, printed in 9-point font, listing five steps no one ever reads. No sudden meltdowns, no heroic fixes—just two people talking while the clock ticks and the labels keep counting down to the next misfire.
dialogue:
Nkechi: The printer skips every seventh tag. Can you fix it?
Florian: You’ll want the IT ticket portal, not me.
Nkechi: Portal takes three days. I need the rack done by eight.
Florian: Talk to the day shift lead, then.
Nkechi: Day shift isn’t here. You’re here.
Florian: I’m off the clock in four minutes.
Nkechi: Then tell me what to press in the next four minutes.
Florian: Hold the feed button till the light flashes twice.
Nkechi: Did that already. Still skips.
Florian: Then the roller’s greasy. Clean it.
Nkechi: Wiped it twice. Still skips.
Florian: Swab the sensor eye, left corner.
Nkechi: Done. Still skips.
Florian: Power-cycle the whole rack, then.
Nkechi: That dumps the queue. I lose the order.
Florian: Better than losing the seventh tube every rack.
Nkechi: There’s got to be a setting.
Florian: Settings are behind the admin login.
Nkechi: You have the login.
Florian: I’m not authorized for firmware.
Nkechi: So I’m stuck doing manual labels.
Florian: Until the portal ticket closes, yeah.

“You’ll want the IT ticket portal, not me.”

Nkechi’s jaw tightened. She tapped the tray, emphasizing the urgency. “Portal takes three days. I need the rack done by eight.”

Florian shifted his weight, the floorboards creaking under his boot. He pointed vaguely toward the empty office. “Talk to the day shift lead, then.”

“Day shift isn’t here. You’re here.”

He sighed, a short exhale through his nose. “I’m off the clock in four minutes.”

Nkechi stepped closer, invading the small circle of light beneath the lamp. “Then tell me what to press in the next four minutes.”

Florian straightened, just enough to look her in the eye. “Hold the feed button till the light flashes twice.”

She moved to the machine, fingers flying. A moment later, she stepped back, arms crossed. “Did that already. Still skips.”

“Then the roller’s greasy. Clean it.”

She produced a wipe, scrubbed the mechanism with practiced efficiency, and returned the cloth to her pocket. “Wiped it twice. Still skips.”

Florian rubbed the back of his neck. “Swab the sensor eye, left corner.”

Nkechi obeyed, leaning in to inspect the tiny lens. She pulled back, frustration etching lines into her forehead. “Done. Still skips.”

“Power-cycle the whole rack, then.”

Nkechi froze. Her hand hovered over the power switch. “That dumps the queue. I lose the order.”

Florian shrugged, checking his watch again. The sun had risen another degree; his bike lock might be thawing. “Better than losing the seventh tube every rack.”

“There’s got to be a setting.”

“Settings are behind the admin login.”

Nkechi’s eyes narrowed, fixing on him. “You have the login.”

Florian shook his head slowly, stepping back toward the door. “I’m not authorized for firmware.”

She looked at the jammed printer, then at the stack of unlabeled tubes. Defeat settled over her like a cold coat. “So I’m stuck doing manual labels.”

Florian opened the door. The hallway air rushed in, cold and quiet. “Until the portal ticket closes, yeah.”

The lesson booth sits at the back of a music store that smells like old varnish and fluorescent anxiety, mid-afternoon on a Thursday when the parking meter outside demands migration. The walls are crowded with hanging mandolins—F-styles and A-styles dangling from pegs like copper-colored bats—creating a canopy that presses down on the two occupants. The carpet is worn flat where countless students have tapped their feet, and a metronome sits silent on the laminate shelf, its battery long dead.

Orin stands with his own mandolin case at his feet, a graduate student in ethnomusicology who has spent three weeks grinding tremolo exercises until his right wrist speaks in sharp Morse code pain. He approached Pallavi by reputation—she gives bluegrass lessons here on Thursdays—and he wants a surgical fix: angle adjustments, muscle mechanics, the physics of endurance. He is polite by breeding but his patience has the half-life of a mayfly; he can see her jacket is already on, her keys threaded through her fingers, and he knows before he asks that he is an inconvenience.

Pallavi leans against the wall with her coat collar up, her gig bag already packed and slung diagonal across her chest. She teaches here for the discount on strings, not for missionary work, and she has a lineup gig across the bridge in forty minutes. She resents the ambush. Her strategy is to remain cordial but mobile, offering deflections shaped like advice—vague platitudes about "feeling the motion" and "staying loose"—without ever stepping into the actual mechanics of wrist rotation or forearm anchoring. She will redirect him to YouTube, to Greg who teaches Tuesdays, to the concept of rest, anything that keeps the conversation from requiring her to demonstrate or explain. The keys in her left hand jingle when she shifts her weight, a small auditory clock counting down to her escape.

The arc is simple and grinding: Orin pushes for concrete technique, Pallavi offers mist, and the gap between them widens until the only resolution is her leaving. No miracles occur, no breakthrough happens. The mandolins hang silent above, witnesses to a transaction that never completes.

Orin frowned, the frustration tightening his jaw. “That’s not a technique. I’m doing something wrong mechanically. Is it the angle or the forearm support?”

She shrugged, the movement slight and dismissive. “Honestly, lots of people overthink it. Just try to stay loose.”

“I am trying.” Orin stepped closer, his voice rising slightly. “I’m asking for specific adjustments. Pick position, wrist height, something concrete?”

Pallavi glanced at the dead metronome on the shelf, then back to him, her expression placid. “There’s some really good breakdowns on YouTube if you search ‘mandolin tremolo technique.’ Might be better than me explaining it.”

“Fine.” Orin cut her off, desperation edging his tone. “One thing: do I pivot from the elbow or keep the forearm locked?”

“Have you tried just taking a break every five minutes?” Pallavi offered, a thin smile touching her lips. “Rest is important.”

“That’s prevention, not technique.” Orin’s eyes narrowed. “You’re not hearing my actual question.”

“I hear you, I just think maybe you need to approach it differently.” She unhooked her keys from her belt loop, the metal clicking. “Anyway, my car’s parked at a meter.”

The package room sat in the basement of the 1960s apartment block, a concrete box lit by two strips of fluorescent tubes that hummed like tired bees. Rows of steel lockers lined the walls, each door a square mouth waiting for Amazon, FedEx, or the occasional Thai take-out bag. It was four-thirty on a Tuesday afternoon, the dead hour when most tenants were still at work, so the air smelled only of floor wax and the faint metallic breath of the lockers themselves.

Renzo stood in front of locker 14B, jaw tight, one finger stabbing the scanner for the fourth time. The red light kept blinking, the package inside still untracked and, technically, undelivered. His dissertation folder was thirty pages heavier than it had been this morning, and the department deadline was tomorrow at five. He needed the hand-off to register so he could get back upstairs and keep typing.

Polina leaned against the opposite wall, coat already on, car keys in her hand. She had come down to grab a parcel of her own and was halfway out the door when Renzo blocked the exit with a polite, clipped question. The toe of her right boot tapped once against the tile: a small, audible sigh in leather.

A sticker on the locker door asked for “Level-2 diagnostics,” whatever that meant, and Renzo’s patience was thinning like ice in April. Polina’s answers, when they came, were short, pointed toward the ceiling, and always ended with the same shrug: “Try the super.” She didn’t want to be the super, not today.

story:
Renzo pressed his thumb against the cold steel of locker 14B, the red LED on the scanner blinking with a rhythm that felt personally offensive. The hum of the fluorescents drilled into his skull, matching the pulse in his temples. He needed this package scanned, logged, and forgotten so he could return to the dissertation that was eating his life. Polina stood near the exit, one hand on the door handle, her keys jingling softly against her palm. She watched him with the detached interest of someone observing a minor mechanical failure in a stranger’s life.

“The scanner keeps rejecting the barcode. Any idea why?”

Polina didn’t move toward him. She kept her weight on her left foot, eyes scanning the corridor above the lockers. “Did you try wiping the lens?”

Renzo scrubbed at the black plastic with his sleeve, the fabric rough against the grime. “Twice. Still flashing red.”

“Sometimes the firmware stalls. Reboot it.” Her voice was flat, offering the advice without the weight of conviction.

Renzo ran a hand over the smooth metal door, searching for seams. “How? There's no power button.”

Polina shifted her keys from one hand to the other, the metal clicking against her ring. “Management left a reset hole on the side. Paperclip.”

Renzo frowned, studying the edge of the unit. “You're sure that won't brick the locker?”

Polina shrugged, a small, sharp movement of her shoulders under her coat. “If it does, the super deals with it, not me.”

Renzo leaned in, squinting at the paneling. “Where's the reset hole exactly?”

“Bottom right corner, under the sticker.” She pointed with her chin, not her hand, indicating the faded yellow label that promised ‘Level-2 diagnostics.’

He bent, knees popping, and wedged a straightened paperclip into the tiny recess. He pushed, waited, pulled. “I've jammed the clip in. Nothing.”

Polina checked her watch, the glow illuminating the lines around her eyes. “Hold it ten seconds, then let the board cycle.”

Renzo counted under his breath, the sound of his own breathing loud in the small room. One, two, three… ten. He withdrew the clip. The light remained a steady, accusatory crimson. “Light's still red. Could the barcode be the issue?”

“Could be. Wrong label, crinkles, low contrast.” She turned her body slightly, angling toward the door as if preparing to leave him to his fate.

Renzo picked up the box, turning it over in his hands. The label was flat, crisp, and perfectly aligned. “Label looks fine. What else?”

Polina paused, her hand still on the knob. She glanced at the open locker, peering into the dark void. “Package too far back. Sensor can't read through plastic.”

Renzo looked at the depth of the shelf, then back at the scanner. “So shift the box forward?”

“Or tape the barcode where the beam hits.”

Renzo tore a strip of packing tape from the roll on the floor, stuck the label to the front of the inner cardboard flap, and presented it to the sensor. The light turned green. A soft chime echoed in the concrete box.

“That worked. Thanks.”

Polina’s expression didn’t change, but her shoulders relaxed a fraction. “No problem. Shut the door gently.”

Renzo pushed the steel door until it clicked shut, the sound final and satisfying. Polina stepped out into the hallway, the fluorescent buzz fading behind her as the door swung closed.

Setting: Interior of the emergency-app testing lab. Post-lunch lull, 1:42 p.m. The room smells of burnt popcorn and the over-warm tang of server racks exhaling hot air. A bank of standing-desk monitors scrolls fake heat maps of a fictional wildfire pushing toward neighborhoods made of greyscale polygons. Fluorescent lights buzz overhead, one tube ready to blink out. Sawyer stands by workstation 7 wearing noise-canceling headphones pushed back around his neck; the strap is frayed where the plastic cracked last fall. Under the desk sits a worn yellow hill-crest backpack leaking granola-bar wrappers. Meera leans against the doorway threshold, coat already buttoned, one foot turned toward the hall that leads to the exit stair. A faint aroma of petrol clings to her jeans—the lab's parking lot generator had sputtered diesel twenty minutes ago when the demo finished.

Sawyer's state: Last two weeks wading through encrypted test-logs; needs a concrete answer in the next ten minutes so he can email the final report before his supervising prof boards a plane. Meera's state: Two full shifts back-to-back on simulation runs; eyes feel like sand. Wants coffee and the bus. Has already slid her ID badge off the lanyard and into her pocket. Conversation needed ending before it started.

Key objects to anchor on: (1) The lab's shared log server glowing amber on its tiny amber status LED—fine place to check but Meera will never say so. (2) The coat-cue in her hand: sleeves halfway on, ready to flee. Sawyer's questions will nudge against these items as he looks for traction.

Dramatic arc: Help-seeker presses, helper side-steps every concrete cue; exchange shortens by degrees until Sawyer either yields to deflection or runs out of time. No twists—just friction and mutual awareness that this will not resolve.

Whitney's patience for explanations is thin after a semester of faculty meetings; she wants two sentences of guidance, not a saga. Ulric's posture says he'd rather be anywhere else: shoulders angled toward the exit, head half-turned as if listening for a bell only he can hear. He keeps his answers clipped, his gaze on the clock above the freezer, and the conversation short. On the table between them: one jar of raspberry jam, one ballpoint pen, one half-used roll of gummed labels, faint strawberry stains on the edge like a crime scene. The encounter is simple: student asks for help, helper declines politely and redirects, twice; the jar stays unlabeled, the clock ticks.

The air hung heavy with the cloying scent of boiled fruit and the waxy perfume of paraffin wax. Whitney stood beside the table, a half-used roll of gummed labels unspooled before her, a hand-inked sample tacky between her fingers. She adjusted her glasses, eyes scanning the room for an exit from the logistical dead end. Ulric leaned against the wall near the back stairs, a mop handle resting lightly on his shoulder, car keys jingling softly against the metal bucket at his feet. He stared at the clock above the freezer, his posture angled toward the door, head tilted as if listening for a bell only he could hear.

“Got a minute? I need to print labels for these jars by Sunday.”

Ulric didn’t look up from the clock. “Talk to Brenda. She handles graphics.”

Whitney’s jaw tightened slightly; she had spent three hours on hold earlier. “Brenda's in Cincinnati until Thursday.”

He shifted his weight, the rubber sole of his boot squeaking on the linoleum. “Then ask Derek in the office. He has the template.”

“Derek said the printer only does black and white.”

“They taste what's inside. Skip the graphics.” He finally glanced at the jars, his expression flat.

Whitney picked up a jar, turning it in the dim light. “I need color to match the fruit. Customers read labels first.”

“People buy jam, not posters. Black and white works.” He tapped his wrist, checking the time again.

“The sale's on Sunday. I can't show up empty-handed.”

“Handwrite them. Sharpie on the lid is fine.” He reached for the keys at his belt, the jingle sharp in the quiet room.

“Forty-eight jars, sixty cents each. I want them to look professional.”

“Stickers cost more than the profit margin. Move on.” His hand hovered over the doorknob.

“Church logo belongs on the label. It's a branding issue.” Whitney’s voice remained steady, though her fingers tightened around the jar.

“Treasury keeps the logo file. They're closed Tuesdays.” He looked at her, then back at the door.

“I can email them tonight.”

“They meet again next month. Ask then.”

“Jam spoils before next month.” The sour-sweet smell seemed to intensify as the air grew still.

“Sell it unlabeled. Call it rustic.” He shrugged, one shoulder lifting.

“Customers ask what kind of jelly.”

“Tell them mystery. They'll still buy.” He pushed off the wall, taking a step toward the stairs.

“I need ingredients listed for allergies.” Whitney held up the pen, the cap still on.

“Print the list on scrap paper. Tape it to the table.”

“People take jars home.”

plan:
Late afternoon in the raftered wardrobe loft above the community children’s theater. Sun slats in through the single dormer, catching the glitter on the floorboards so every footstep makes a tiny star-burst. Racks of panto costumes hulk like sleeping gryphons; a papier-mâché dragon head stares with one peeled-off eye. The air tastes of hot glue and old hairspray.

Talulah, still in jeans after a day of rehearsal notes, climbs the last rung gripping a plastic grocery bag full of white lace wings. She’s on a grant deadline to finish her thesis project: a wearable fairy rig that can survive a thirty-minute children’s show and a post-show Q-and-A. Her adviser wants “delicate but indestructible.” The glue she tried last week cracked like thin ice; the starch the week before went floppy at the first sweat. She needs a quick, reliable method and she’s already late for the tech fitting downstairs.

Urielis sits on a cedar chest threading elastic through a dwarf beard. They inherited this loft when the city cut the crafts budget; now they fix whatever props wander up the stairs and they like the quiet. They’re due at a life-drawing class in forty minutes—figure modelling pays better than costumes ever did—and they’ve left their bus ticket on the windowsill. Their mind is already on the commute and whether the radiator at the studio has finally been fixed.

Objects that matter: the half-finished dwarf beard (a soft, safe prop to fiddle with), an open tin of fabric stiffener on the worktable (label visible: Flexible—won’t crack), and the grocery bag of lace wings Talulah keeps lifting like evidence.

The encounter arcs simply: Talulah asks; Urielis deflects, redirects, never quite answers; Talulah presses once more, realizes she’s getting the brush-off, and the discussion closes with her deciding to try the supply cupboard herself while Urielis folds the beard, pockets the bus ticket, and heads for the stairs.

Urielis paused the needle, letting it hang in the thread. “Not really my department. You want the paint-shop downstairs.”

Talulah shifted her weight, the ladder creaking. The wings in her bag rustled, fragile as breath. “I tried paint-shop acrylic medium—it cracked the second rehearsal. I need something with give.”

Urielis resumed threading, the motion rhythmic, ignoring the tension in the small space. “Hobby store sells spray stiffener. Bottle says ‘fabric-friendly.’”

“It went limp after ten minutes onstage under hot lights.” Talulah lifted the bag slightly, as if showing evidence in court.

Urielis shrugged, one shoulder rising under a faded sweater. “Huh. Maybe ask wardrobe at the opera company? They deal with wings.”

“Their union doesn’t talk to students without faculty signature. Takes weeks. My tech is tomorrow.” Talulah’s grip tightened on the bag handle.

“Rough.” Urielis pulled the thread taut. “You could sew wire along the edges. Quick and dirty.”

Talulah shook her head, a strand of hair escaping her bun. “Director says no metal; kids grab everything. Also the lace tears.”

Urielis finally looked up, eyes scanning the shelves before dropping back to the beard. “Then maybe just accept floppy wings. Kids won’t notice.”

“They notice. I notice. There has to be a middle ground.” She stepped down, landing with a soft thud on the glitter-dusted floorboards.

Urielis stood, brushing lint from their knees. “Google ‘fabric taxidermy.’ I’ve heard that works.”

Talulah exhaled sharply, looking at the chaotic shelves around them. “I’ve googled. That’s where I got the starch recipe that failed yesterday. Anything else on this shelf?”

Urielis picked up the bus ticket from the sill, sliding it into a pocket. “Probably, but I’m off the clock. Life-drawing starts in half an hour.”

Talulah spotted an open tin on the worktable, the label bold and promising. She pointed at it. “One more minute. Have you used that tin? The one labeled ‘Flexible—won’t crack’?”

Urielis glanced at it, then at the door. “Bought it for astronaut scenery, never tried it on lace. Might bleed.”

Talulah stared at the tin, then at Urielis, who was already turning toward the stairs. “So you don’t know. Great. Thanks for the definite non-answer.”

Urielis didn’t pause, hand on the banister. “Any time. Good luck with the fairies.”

Mid-afternoon, mid-September. Sun still high enough to fry the tops of your ears, but sliding west behind the campus security office so the three experimental parking bays sit long-shadowed and too quiet. The storm-water demo strip is crushed limestone edged with temporary plastic curbing, still holding the heat of the day like a skillet. A pallet of gray-blue gravel sits beside the bay labelled "Site B," shrink-wrap rattling in the breeze, a yellow shipping tag flapping Morse code. Off to the side: a dented wheelbarrow, half-full of #57 stone, looks like someone forgot it mid-shift.

Mirek shoves his phone back in his jeans pocket after checking a lab-readout photo from this morning's infiltration test. He's thirty minutes behind schedule, grant figures due tomorrow, and the thesis advisor keeps texting "Clarify aggregate mix." All he needs is a straight answer about whether the permeability trade-off with 3/8-inch chip is worth the stripping risk when campus maintenance inevitably runs plows over it by February.

Enter Safa, leaning on a broom by the maintenance shed door, clearly on the docket for end-of-shift cleanup. Boots still caked with drywall dust from the residence-hall reno—picture the crumbs stuck in the tread like broken snow. Safa has one earbud in, volume loud enough the percussion leaks tinny, and keeps glancing at the wall clock visible through the employee door twenty paces away: shift ends in fourteen minutes. Motivation: finish load-out, clock out, avoid all new tasks invented at 4:46 p.m. This conversation is fundamentally low on their priority list, and their answers will be shaped accordingly.

The dramatic shape is simply one person trying politely but urgently to extract practical information; the other person deflects with increasing brevity until the first person gives up and concludes the interaction without resolution. No explosions, no breakthrough epiphanies—just a slow leak of Mirek's optimism happening one clipped syllable at a time.

Safa: Didn't keep the paperwork. Shrunk it all up in the loader and rolled on.

Safa: Eyeball's about done for today. Got kitchen duty at six.

Safa: Respectfully, mister, gravel is gravel. Looks like gravel, acts like gravel.

Safa: Feel free to borrow the rig. Everything's labeled wrong anyway.

Safa: All yours, and the broom's by the door when you're done.

plan:
Dawn's still two hours off, but the ovens in "Panecillo's" are already clucking like grudging hens. Nerea stands on the customer side of the scarred pine counter, laptop bag slung over one shoulder, backpack drooping from the other. Fluorescent lights buzz overhead, giving everything the color of missed sleep. Behind her, the glass door advertising "Hot Bread at 5 A.M." is locked; nobody's supposed to be inside but the baker. 

She's come from a night coding session at the library—the code never ran, the class credit feels flimsy, and now she's picturing her follower count the way other people picture their credit card balances. Posting her grandmother's orange-brioche recipe—that fragrant, porous thing Nerea still calls "la suerte"—could pay rent. Or, says the nagging lump under her ribs, it could turn something stitched into family birthdays into one more disposable pin.

The only soul visible is Bosco, early-shift oven man, late-shift nothing man. He's wiping shortening from beneath his fingernails. He's got a lunchbox under one arm and the rhythm of someone who wants the floor remembered, not the conversation. 

Objects that'll matter: a navy-blue Polaroid camera taped to a shelf for "quality shots" never taken; the clipboard of yesterday's order sheet with scribbled notes like "need more foam trays."

Dramatic shape: Nerea asks for a sounding board. Bosco provides exactly one plank and suggests someone else's dock. No shouting. Just the stall and drift toward silence while the room fills with the yeasty heat of a third rack of loaves.
dialogue:
Nerea: If I put the orange-brioche recipe online, does that make it less ours?
Bosco: Dunno. Copyright office opens at nine; they’ll explain the treadmill.
Nerea: I'm not talking law. I mean—will people treat it like just another click?
Bosco: Folks click on what they want. My cousin lost a finger to a table saw, still posts pictures.
Nerea: So you're saying the recipe's already public once the first neighbor tastes it?
Bosco: More like once the smell leaves the door, every alley cat thinks it's their supper.
Nerea: Then what protects the story tied to it?
Bosco: You’re asking the wrong apron. Marketing majors upstairs run evenings.
Nerea: You know the difference between sharing and stripping, though.
Bosco: Mostly I know the difference between dough that doubles and dough that don’t. Clock’s ticking.
Nerea: Tick loud enough to drown the question, then?
Bosco: Tick’s all I got. You want a mentor, grab Joaquin at the kneading bench—he comes in noonish.
Nerea: Noon’s too late; the post drafts up at six.
Bosco: Draft sounds fast; good luck steering it.
Nerea: I thought maybe the smell, the paper she wrote it on, something would stay sacred.
Bosco: Sacred stuff usually isn’t the recipe. Usually the table around it.

plan:
Steam hit the rafters of the sugar shack at four in the afternoon, the day’s boil tailing off. Sienna stood by the evaporator, one glove off, tapping a blistered spot on the corner of the stainless pan. She had three hours of sleep, a data set due at midnight, and a pint that tasted like burnt sugar. Somewhere behind her, a kettle hissed.

Bogdan had one foot out the door, jacket half-zipped, phone pinging with a ride that had already waited too long. He kept his distance from the arch of heat, thumbs in pockets, eyes on the clock like it might save him.

Between them, the air smelled of scorched sap and hot metal. A stack of metal deflectors—thin as razor blades—sat on the bench, unused. The thermometer in the draw-off box still read two hundred and twenty-seven. The question in the room wanted to know why the syrup kept turning bitter at the edges before it ever reached the centre.
dialogue:
Sienna: The front left corner keeps caramelizing before the rest even hits syrup. What shifts the heat?
Bogdan: Check the partition plate. If it’s warped, you get a hot pocket. I’ve got a ride waiting.
Sienna: Plate’s flat. I flipped it, same burn pattern underneath. Could the flame angle be off?
Bogdan: Could be. Could also be the draw-off valve throttling late. Try calling the supplier. They have specs.
Sienna: Supplier sent me here. You’re the one standing next to the rig. What’s your gut read?
Bogdan: Gut says I’m late. Look, slide the stack forward an inch, drop the firebox half a notch, see if the colour evens out. I need to move.
Sienna: Tried sliding. Colour stayed streaked. If I drop the box, I lose boil rate. Trade-off worth it?
Bogdan: Depends if you want speed or flavour. Pick one. I’ve got someone double-parked outside.
Sienna: I want both. That’s why I’m asking. You run this rig last season. What’d you tweak?
Bogdan: Last season I ran a different rig. Swapped the front pan for a deeper one. You don’t have that. Ask Ernie—he’s still around.
Sienna: Ernie’s shed is locked. Keys are with you, according to the board. Can you unlock it?
Bogdan: Keys are in the office. Office closes at five. It’s four fifty-eight. I’m walking away now.
Sienna: Thirty seconds. Give me the short version. What keeps the corner from scorching?
Bogdan: Lower the corner. Or raise the rest. Physics doesn’t care which. Try a brick. Later.
Sienna: Brick under the back left jack? That tilts the whole arch. Sap runs thinner uphill. You sure?
Bogdan: Sure I’m late. Tilt or burn. Your call. I’m gone. Door’s open when you leave.
Sienna: Thanks for almost nothing.
Bogdan: Welcome. Close the door behind you. Lights switch off automatic.

Wednesday, 2:17 p.m. The scanning room is half broom closet, half sci-fi prop cupboard: one wall of pegboard crammed with spare cuffs, a plastic foot soaking in milky detergent, and the squat white 3-D scanner that hums like a refrigerator with insomnia. A gluey scent of medical adhesive clings to everything, overlaid by the tang of burnt electronics from yesterday’s recalibration gone wrong. Fluorescent tubes buzz overhead, throwing a light so flat it erases skin pores.

Jasmin: fourth-year biomech Ph.D., here on her own dime to digitize a prosthetic socket. Her grant expires in thirty-one days; she needs this print perfect on first pass. She’s already taped sixteen reflective dots to the rim of the limb mold and recorded ten slow revolutions on the turntable. Now she’s worried the capture is grainy. She wants a quick, expert thumbs-up or a fix.

Kenji: technician who officially signs off the scans but hasn’t been paid overtime in six months. Mind currently parked on the fish-taco truck idling outside the staff gate, which closes in four minutes. He keeps wiping his palms on his cargo pants, keys jangling against his belt.

Environmental props: the scanner’s green status bar flickering at 0.45 mm/pixel; a half-used roll of retro-reflective tape on the counter; the blinking wall clock nudging 14:20.

Dramatic shape: straightforward request → practiced deflection → repeated request → shorter deflections and hints that another authority exists elsewhere. The interaction ends without resolution; Kenji exits for tacos, Jasmin is left staring at the glow of an unconfirmed file.
dialogue:
Jasmin: Does that density look good enough for printing? It’s holding at 0.45 millimeters.
Kenji: Prints happen downstairs. I just run the scan.
Jasmin: Right, but if the mesh is sparse now the socket will warp. Can you bump the resolution?
Kenji: Talk to Fab; they’ve got a laser booth that hits sub-point-two.
Jasmin: Fab’s booked until Friday. My grant clock runs out at five. Any tweaks I can do here?
Kenji: Not in the software I’ve got. You’d need the research license.
Jasmin: Which is on the computer behind you. Could we open it?
Kenji: Needs a PI login. Can’t hand that out.
Jasmin: I’m the PI on this protocol. Here’s my card.
Kenji: Still needs departmental approval in the system. Forms go to McNamera.
Jasmin: McNamera’s in Minneapolis all week. There must be a workaround.
Kenji: You could email tech support. Ticket desk closes at three.
Jasmin: I’m looking at thirty seconds of your time. Just hit override and re-scan.
Kenji: Board policy says no re-scans without written justification.
Jasmin: Written where? A sticky note? Email? Carrier pigeon?
Kenji: Use the request form on the portal; it’s under Resources.
Jasmin: Portal’s down for maintenance. The alert’s on your own homepage.
Kenji: Then try again tomorrow. Scanner books are lighter in the mornings.
Jasmin: The prosthesis ships tomorrow morning. I need the file verified now.
Kenji: I hear you; wish I could bend the rules but my hands are tied.
Jasmin: So you’re telling me a one-minute toggle is impossible?
Kenji: Not impossible—just above my clearance. Sorry.
Jasmin: Fine. I’ll find someone qualified to help. Thanks… for almost nothing.
Kenji: No problem. Good luck.
story:
Jasmin leaned over the squat white scanner, its hum vibrating through the laminate counter like a refrigerator suffering from insomnia. Sixteen reflective dots stared back at her from the prosthetic socket mold, a constellation of cheap plastic hope. The air tasted of burnt electronics and stale adhesive, a cocktail of yesterday’s failed recalibration. She tapped the screen, where the green status bar flickered at 0.45 mm/pixel.

“Does that density look good enough for printing?” Jasmin asked. “It’s holding at 0.45 millimeters.”

Kenji stood by the door, keys jangling a rhythmic counterpoint to the fluorescent buzz. He wiped a palm on his cargo pants, eyes drifting to the clock: 2:19. “Prints happen downstairs. I just run the scan.”

Jasmin straightened, the grant deadline looming like a physical weight. “Right, but if the mesh is sparse now the socket will warp. Can you bump the resolution?”

He didn’t look at the screen. “Talk to Fab; they’ve got a laser booth that hits sub-point-two.”

“Fab’s booked until Friday. My grant clock runs out at five. Any tweaks I can do here?”

Kenji shifted his weight, the floorboard groaning. “Not in the software I’ve got. You’d need the research license.”

She gestured to the terminal behind him, its screen dark but accessible. “Which is on the computer behind you. Could we open it?”

“Needs a PI login. Can’t hand that out.”

“I’m the PI on this protocol. Here’s my card.” She slid it across the counter, plastic clicking against the surface.

Kenji didn’t take it. “Still needs departmental approval in the system. Forms go to McNamera.”

“McNamera’s in Minneapolis all week. There must be a workaround.”

“You could email tech support. Ticket desk closes at three.”

Her jaw tightened. “I’m looking at thirty seconds of your time. Just hit override and re-scan.”

“Board policy says no re-scans without written justification.”

“Written where? A sticky note? Email? Carrier pigeon?”

“Use the request form on the portal; it’s under Resources.”

Jasmin pointed to the browser window open on his monitor, the red banner unmistakable. “Portal’s down for maintenance. The alert’s on your own homepage.”

Kenji checked his watch again. The fish-taco truck was idling outside, exhaust puffing into the afternoon chill. “Then try again tomorrow. Scanner books are lighter in the mornings.”

“The prosthesis ships tomorrow morning. I need the file verified now.”

“I hear you; wish I could bend the rules but my hands are tied.” He pulled his keys free, the metal bright and final.

“So you’re telling me a one-minute toggle is impossible?”

“Not impossible—just above my clearance. Sorry.”

Jasmin stared at the unverified file, the green bar still flickering. “Fine. I’ll find someone qualified to help. Thanks… for almost nothing.”

Kenji was already at the door, hand on the latch. “No problem. Good luck.”

He slipped out, leaving Jasmin alone with the hum and the gluey scent, the clock ticking toward 2:20.
